A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MAS-Bench and retain identifiable tasks, agents, experiments, and shortcut-generation methods. The main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original agent evaluations, shortcut-generation comparisons, difficulty analyses, and failure cases, including Tables 2, 3, 5, and 7.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds model comparisons, shortcut-interference tests, cross-version validation, and automated-evaluator validation against human judgments.

M1.justification: The hybrid agents and shortcut-generation procedures are retained; additional model families explicitly use the same shortcut injection strategy. However, v2 specifies the two-stage MAS-Bench-Eval pipeline, while v1 only briefly describes a SPA-Bench adaptation. The PDFs do not establish whether this changes the evaluator's procedure or documents its existing implementation.

E1.justification: The 139 tasks, 11 applications, and 69-task shortcut-generation subset remain. v2 adds targeted environmental conditions: irrelevant-only shortcut pools on 23 existing cross-app tasks and shortcut testing across at least five versions of each application.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands the evaluated comparators with Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, GLM-4.5V, UI-TARS-1.5, GUI-Owl, ScaleCUA, and MAI-UI models, including matched MAS variants where supported. Earlier workflow baselines and the shortcut-generation comparator set in Table 3 remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds ground-truth shortcut-selection scoring, a controlled relevant-shortcut removal protocol, and automated-versus-human evaluation on 278 trajectories. The original task and shortcut-generation evaluation designs remain. The advertised seven-to-nine metric count largely consolidates measures already used in v1.

E4.justification: New analyses examine shortcut-selection precision and redundancy, resistance to irrelevant shortcuts, stability across application versions, and automated scoring reliability. These address substantial robustness and measurement-validity questions absent from v1. Earlier difficulty analyses and failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: v2 newly documents three independent human demonstrations per task and selection of their minimum step count for the human baseline (Appendix A.5). This adds replication and aggregation information without establishing increased runs. Neither version reports agent seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive model, interference, and evaluator results, including MAS-GLM-4.5V's 68.3% overall success rate. Retained results also change: Gemini-2.0-Flash MAS-MobileAgent's cross-app MSRS changes from 0.738 to 0.938 in Table 5, and several difficulty-level values change. Shortcut-generation Table 3 remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The written action-ratio definition changes from GUI operations divided by shortcut operations (GSAR) to shortcut operations divided by GUI operations (S2GR; v2 Appendix A.6). This corrects a mathematical definition beyond renaming, although many reported ratios remain identical. No theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The central benchmark and shortcut-generation contributions remain. v2 broadens the stated contribution to comparisons across workflow, general-purpose, and specialized GUI agents, explicitly adds exposing shortcut misuse, and frames predefined structural shortcuts as a reference upper bound.

C2.justification: v1's broad finding that weaker models benefit more becomes a qualified account involving nonmonotonic model-size effects and reliable shortcut selection. v2 also discusses specialized-model failures, controlled retrieval, application-version stability, emulator-only evaluation, and evaluator limitations, materially sharpening applicability and failure conditions.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies snapshot resets, isolated test accounts, GPU hardware, intent-accessible ADB endpoints, UI-tree-based RPA, application-keyword retrieval, prompt injection, human-baseline collection, and Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro evaluator roles. These substantially expand implementation disclosure without necessarily establishing changes to existing procedures.

R1.justification: The cited literature is substantially revised, adding newer general-purpose and specialized GUI-model families while removing much earlier automation, testing, and survey literature. Automated evaluation also shifts from an explicitly attributed SPA-Bench adaptation to a separately named MAS-Bench-Eval protocol. The central hybrid-benchmark positioning remains.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the exposition: detailed metrics move to Appendix A.6, experiments separate setup and protocols, and appendices reorganize implementation, detailed results, and evaluator reliability. The abstract, findings, and interpretations are revised, and limitations become a standalone section.

P2.justification: Table 2 becomes a grouped overall comparison with relative-change annotations, while expanded single-app and cross-app breakdowns appear in Tables 9 and 10. v2 adds task-category, metric-summary, robustness, and reliability tables plus evaluator Figure 7. Existing workflow and failure figures are largely retained or relocated within a reformatted layout.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited baseline coverage and unvalidated automated scoring through broader comparisons, shortcut-misuse tests, and human-validation results. Added implementation details and qualified interpretations strengthen reproducibility and credibility. Reporting inconsistencies temper these gains: v2 Tables 5 and 10 disagree on some cross-app values, and Section 3.7 presents single-app validation figures as covering the full sample. Nevertheless, the added evidence resolves important weaknesses in v1.
